newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Tariffs seen boosting Zimbabwe industry in time.
newsitem.headline: Tariffs seen boosting Zimbabwe industry in time.

text.p: Zimbabwe has tried to boost investment by scrapping import duty on capital goods and deeply cutting tax on raw materials and spares from March 1.
But industry and economic analysts say the impact of the tariff regime unveiled by President Robert Mugabe's government last Friday will take at least a year to realise.

"Like many investment incentives, the results are not going to come overnight. Overall, the (industry's) mood has improved greatly, but let's see how that translates itself on the ground," said Edmore Tobaiwa, chief economist at the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce (ZNCC).
"Capital projects take some time and we can only tell from the next 12 months, if not a longer period," he told Reuters.

Many Zimbabwean manufacturing companies are limping on old machinery and technology, and had complained it was expensive to retool because of high import duties and interest rates, which have now fallen to around 18 percent from 28 percent a year ago.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa abolished the 25 percent import tax on capital goods and slashed duties on raw materials for manufacturing to five percent from 40 percent.

Duty on industrial spares was cut to 15 percent from up to 56 percent and on partly processed inputs to 15 percent from up to 55 percent, in a package aimed at boosting investment, exports and general economic growth.

To protect local industry, Murerwa said finished imported goods would attract duty of 40 to 85 percent, from zero to 85 percent, with the highest tariffs on electronics, batteries, textiles and clothing.
The new taxes do not apply where the southern African country has preferential trading pacts, including South Africa with which it is negotiating a crucial economic agreement.

"Without South Africa, its impact, in the short-term, in controlling imports will be very limited," said Charles Rukuni, editor and publisher of an independent political and economic Zimbabwean newsletter, The Insider.
"But in time, we may see the expected domestic investment and expansion," he said.

Zimbabwe has signed an agreement in principle with South Africa requiring Pretoria to restore to about 30 percent duty on Zimbabwean textile and clothing exports, which it tripled in 1992 to protect its industry.
The South African move crippled Zimbabwe's industry, and Zimbabwe has since been accusing its neighbour and main continental trading partner dumping goods on its market.
The Zimbabwe government announced a new tariff regime last August but withdrew it after a week under pressure from industrialists.

The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries welcomed the new tariffs, but the Zimbabwe Clothing Council said classing fabric as a finished product, and not a raw material, liable to duty of over 85 percent would hurt members.
ZNCC's Tobaiwa said the tariffs would hurt the country's retail sector which depends heavily on imported finished goods.
